nameStory: Atlantic sand crabs get their name from their peculiar lifestyle of burrowing backwards into sandy beaches along the Atlantic coast. They're also called 'mole crabs' because like moles, they spend most of their time hidden underground, popping up only when the waves wash over them. The scientific name 'Emerita' means 'retired' in Latin, referring to their reclusive, buried lifestyle.
description: Atlantic sand crabs are small, oval-shaped crustaceans that look more like tiny armored eggs than typical crabs. They have no claws and are perfectly designed for life in the sandy surf zone of beaches. These little creatures grow to about an inch long and have a smooth, dome-shaped shell that helps them burrow quickly into wet sand. Unlike other crabs that scuttle sideways, sand crabs move backwards and forwards with remarkable speed.

idTips.label: Egg-shaped body
idTips.description: Smooth, oval shell about the size of a large grape with no visible claws or spines - feels hard and slippery when wet

idTips.label: Feathery antennae
idTips.description: Two delicate, feather-like antennae that stick out from the front end, used for filter feeding - they wave gently in the water

idTips.label: Backwards movement
idTips.description: Burrows tail-first into sand with lightning speed when disturbed - you'll see them disappear backwards in a puff of sand

idTips.label: Sandy coloration
idTips.description: Grayish-tan to pale yellow color that perfectly matches wet beach sand - often with tiny sand grains stuck to the shell

idTips.label: No walking legs visible
idTips.description: Unlike other crabs, legs are tucked completely under the body for burrowing - you won't see them sticking out sideways

habitat: Look for Atlantic sand crabs in the active surf zone of sandy beaches throughout coastal New England, especially where waves regularly wash up and down. They prefer the wet, packed sand where waves break and retreat, typically buried just 2-4 inches deep. You'll find them most easily in the swash zone where the water rushes back and forth with each wave.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin moving into shallow waters as temperatures warm. Look for them starting to appear in the surf zone during low tide on warmer spring days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when they're most abundant and easiest to find. Dig gently in wet sand where waves retreat to uncover dozens of them.
seasonality.fall: Still active through early fall but beginning to move to deeper waters. September and early October can still offer good viewing opportunities.
seasonality.winter: Retreat to deeper offshore waters to escape cold temperatures. Rarely found in the surf zone during winter months in New England.

funFact: Atlantic sand crabs are like tiny underwater butterflies - they use their feathery antennae to filter plankton from the water, rapidly unfurling and curling them back up like delicate fans to catch microscopic meals as waves wash over their buried bodies.
confusionNotes: Most people mistake them for clams or other mollusks when they first see the smooth, oval shells in the sand. The key difference is that sand crabs will quickly scurry backwards when disturbed, while clams and other shells either don't move or close up. Remember: if it races backwards into the sand, it's a sand crab!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sand fleas,' these creatures are not fleas at all and don't bite humans - they're actually crabs that have evolved to look completely un-crab-like. The 'flea' name comes from beach fleas (amphipods), which are entirely different small jumping creatures found higher up on the beach.
compareHints: Atlantic sand crabs are the only mole crab species found in New England waters, making identification straightforward within their family. They're most easily confused with small clams or coquina shells, but unlike those mollusks, sand crabs are active animals that burrow rapidly when exposed. Their backwards-burrowing behavior and feathery feeding antennae are unique among New England beach creatures.
